task: Write one sentence of your own using the word pallid. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know pallid should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The motel's pallid wallpaper had faded to the ghost of a pattern.
Pale can be natural and healthy — fair skin, a light sky; it stops short of pallid, which looks drained of color it ought to have.
Cadaverous goes further than pallid — past unhealthy paleness to looking like the dead.

Wan is the faint, drained look of long tiredness or illness, and it nearly always describes a person and hints at the fatigue behind the fading. Pallid is broader in what it can describe: color missing from anything that ought to have some — a face, a sky, old wallpaper — whether fright, sickness, or age did the draining.

Colorless is the plainest statement of fact: no color is present at all. Pallid adds a judgment — the color is missing from something that ought to have it, drained by sickness, fright, or age. Water is simply colorless; a colorless face would be pallid, because a face should have some.

When the star's voice cracked mid-aria, the understudy in the wings went pallid — her cue was suddenly, terrifyingly real — and the stage manager pressed a water bottle into her shaking hand.
Pallid is the right word because her face lost the color it ought to have: fear drained it.
Pale can be a natural, healthy fairness; pallid always implies color that is missing — from fright, sickness, or exhaustion.
Pallid does two jobs: literally, color drained from what should have some — a face, a winter sky, old wallpaper; figuratively, feeble and lifeless, as in a pallid remake of a great film.
Pale is neutral and can be lovely; pallid always diagnoses something missing.
For shock-gray in an instant, ashen is the sharper word.
